\]

for all \(i\), which, since all \(a_i>0\), implies

This value works, since \(64\left(\frac32\right)^3=216\). Therefore the only possible value of \(n\) is \(64\), so the sum of all possible values is

divisors in \(A\), meaning there are \(2^{15}\) total subsets.

- No element has \(a=4\) and no element has \(b=2\): there are \(4\cdot 2=8\) such divisors, giving \(2^8\) subsets.

# The Best Way to Get a Good Night’s Sleep: A Simple Routine That Works

The best way to get a good night’s sleep is not a single trick, but a reliable system that tells your body when it is time to rest. Many people chase quick fixes, such as melatonin, heavy blankets, or complex meditation apps, but the most powerful tool is consistency. Sleep is driven by two main forces: your internal clock and your sleep pressure. When those two work together, falling asleep becomes easier, staying asleep becomes more natural, and waking up feels less like a battle.

The first step is to protect your sleep schedule. Choose a bedtime and wake-up time that give you enough rest, then keep them the same every day, including weekends. This may seem rigid, but it is one of the most effective changes you can make. Your body learns to anticipate sleep when it sees the same routine. Morning light is also essential. Within an hour of waking, get outside or sit near a bright window for at least 10 to 15 minutes. Daylight helps reset your circadian rhythm, making you more alert in the morning and more sleepy at night.

Next, create a wind-down period. About an hour before bed, begin shifting from “doing” to “resting.” Turn down the lights, stop working on demanding tasks, and avoid stressful conversations if possible. Screens are the biggest obstacle for many people because blue light can suppress melatonin and scrolling can keep the mind active. If you must use a device, use night mode, keep brightness low, and choose calmer content. Even better, replace the screen with something analog: a paperback, a soft playlist, stretching, or a few pages of journaling.

Your bedroom should become a sleep sanctuary. Keep it cool, dark, and quiet. Many people sleep best in a room that feels slightly chilly, around 60 to 67 degrees Fahrenheit, though the ideal temperature varies by person. Blackout curtains, an eye mask, and white noise can help if you cannot fully control your environment. The bed should be reserved for sleep and intimacy, not work, gaming, or long hours of worry. If your mind starts racing, use a simple technique: write down tomorrow’s to-do list so your brain can release the task, then focus on slow breathing. A 4-7-8 pattern—inhale for four counts, hold for seven, exhale for eight—can calm the nervous system without requiring years of meditation practice.

Finally, support sleep during the day. Caffeine is a stimulant, so be careful with coffee, tea, soda, and energy drinks, especially after early afternoon. Alcohol may make you drowsy, but it often fragments sleep and reduces rest quality. Heavy meals close to bedtime can cause discomfort, while a light snack may be fine if you are hungry. Regular exercise is beneficial, but intense workouts too close to bedtime can be stimulating for some people. Daytime naps are okay if kept short, about 20 minutes, and before early afternoon.

The best way to get a good night’s sleep is to make sleep feel predictable and welcoming. When your schedule is steady, your room is prepared, and your evening is calm, your body does not need to fight the transition into rest. Start with one or two changes this week, track how you feel for a few nights, and build from there. Sleep is not just about feeling tired; it is about creating the conditions that let your mind and body recover fully.

## 4. The Bus That Became a Community Living Room

In many places, the local bus is not just transportation. It is a social space.

Riders have described buses where neighbors greet each other by name, where someone lends a charger to a stranger, where a local musician plays a few songs between stops, or where an entire route becomes known for its regulars. One person’s boring commute is another person’s favorite daily ritual.

There is a strange comfort in that: a city can feel less like a machine and more like a neighborhood when you share a bus with the same people again and again.

## 5. The Unusual Vehicles That Are Technically “Public Transit”

Public transportation does not always mean a standard bus or train. Some of the most memorable rides happen on systems that look like they belong in another era or another genre of story.

Think cable cars climbing steep hills, funiculars that feel like elevators with better views, water taxis that slide between islands, trams running through narrow old-town streets, or rail lines that seem designed more for wonder than efficiency.

These rides are interesting not just because they work, but because they remind us that cities have solved movement in creative ways for centuries.

## 6. The Moment a Stranger Makes the Ride Human

Public transportation is full of small, unexpected kindnesses. A stranger gives up a seat without being asked. Someone points to the right turn. A person helps an elderly rider with a heavy bag. A driver slows down so someone can make the bus.

These moments are tiny, but they matter. In a world where public transit can feel crowded, loud, or stressful, a single act of consideration can make the whole ride feel different.

Sometimes the most interesting thing you see on public transportation is not the city outside. It is the person next to you deciding to be kind.

## 7. The Commute That Shows You a City’s Real Life

Tourists often see a city through landmarks. Commuters see it through routine.

On public transit, you see the city as it actually lives: the bakery opening early, the construction crew moving into position, the students rushing to class, the night-shift worker heading home, the rain pooling in the same spot outside the platform, the same street vendor at the same corner every day.

There is a special kind of truth in that. Public transportation does not show you the city’s postcard image. It shows you the city’s pulse.

## 8. The Ride That Turns a Bad Day Into a Memory

Some of the most interesting public transportation stories are not about luxury or novelty. They are about ordinary rides that suddenly become meaningful.

A ride home after a difficult day. A late train shared with a few other insomniacs. A bus that breaks down and forces everyone to wait together, somehow making the delay feel communal. A window seat on a rainy afternoon that suddenly becomes the best part of the day.

Public transportation has a way of turning small moments into memories simply because they happen in motion, surrounded by other lives.

## Final Thought: Public Transit Is a Moving Archive

If there is one thing that makes public transportation so interesting, it is that it carries more than people. It carries moods, routines, stories, seasons, and the daily rhythm of a city.

A bus is not just a vehicle. A train platform is not just a waiting area. A tram is not just metal and wheels. Together, they form a moving archive of human life, full of small surprises, quiet beauty, and the occasional strange moment you will never forget.

So the next time you ride public transportation, look around. The most interesting thing you see may not be the destination at all. It may be the ride itself.

def file_name_check(file_name):
    """Create a function which takes a string representing a file's name, and returns
    'Yes' if the the file's name is valid, and returns 'No' otherwise.
    A file's name is considered to be valid if and only if all the following conditions 
    are met:
    - There should not be more than three digits ('0'-'9') in the file's name.
    - The file's name contains exactly one dot '.'
    - The substring before the dot should not be empty, and it starts with a letter from 
    the latin alphapet ('a'-'z' and 'A'-'Z').
    - The substring after the dot should be one of these: ['txt', 'exe', 'dll']
    Examples:
    file_name_check("example.txt") # => 'Yes'
    file_name_check("1example.dll") # => 'No' (the name should start with a latin alphapet letter)
    """
    if file_name.count('.') != 1:
        return 'No'

    name, extension = file_name.split('.')

    if not name:
        return 'No'

    first_char = name[0]
    if not (('a' <= first_char <= 'z') or ('A' <= first_char <= 'Z')):
        return 'No'

    if extension not in ('txt', 'exe', 'dll'):
        return 'No'

    digit_count = sum(1 for char in file_name if '0' <= char <= '9')
    if digit_count > 3:
        return 'No'

    return 'Yes'
```

There are \(8\) empty chairs. These \(8\) zeros divide the row into \(9\) gaps of occupied chairs:

\[
\_\,0\,\_\,0\,\_ \cdots 0\,\_
\]

In each gap, we can have \(0,1,\) or \(2\) occupied chairs, but not \(3\), since that would create three consecutive chosen chairs. Thus we need the number of solutions to

\[
x_1+x_2+\cdots+x_9=8
\]

where each \(x_i\in\{0,1,2\}\). This is the coefficient of \(x^8\) in

\[
(1+x+x^2)^9.
\]

Let \(a\) be the number of gaps containing \(2\) chosen chairs. Then the remaining chosen chairs must be distributed as singletons. Since

\[
2a+b=8,
\]

we have \(b=8-2a\), and \(a=0,1,2,3,4\). The number of ways is

\[
\sum_{a=0}^{4} \binom{9}{a}\binom{9-a}{8-2a}.
\]

a=0 &: \binom{9}{0}\binom{9}{8}=9,\\

a=3 &: \binom{9}{3}\binom{6}{2}=84\cdot 15=1260,\\
a=4 &: \binom{9}{4}\binom{5}{0}=126.
\end{aligned}
\]

So

\[
N=9+252+1260+1260+126=2907.
\]

Therefore,

\[
N \bmod 1000 = 2907 \bmod 1000 = 907.
\]

I also think the quote has a playful tone. It does not sound like a strict doctrine. It sounds like a wink. It says that the divine may work through small accidents. A dropped letter may be found by the right person. A missed train may lead to a new path. A familiar song may arrive at the exact moment it is needed. These examples show how life can feel woven. They do not prove a hand is guiding everything. They do show that the imagination can turn a loose event into a meaningful sign.

At the same time I can see why some people would object. If we call every coincidence a sign we may blur the line between truth and desire. We all want our lives to make sense. We want pain to have a reason and joy to feel earned. That longing can push us toward magical thinking. A random event may be dressed up as a message because we need one. This is not always wrong. Human beings are meaning makers. We need stories. We need hope. We need a world that feels connected. The quote can honor that need without forcing a fixed answer on everyone.

The quote also raises the question of anonymity. Why would a divine presence need to hide? One answer is that direct revelation would overwhelm us. If everything were obviously sacred we might take the sacred for granted. We might stop noticing it. We might stop responding to it with care. An anonymous hand leaves room for humility. It leaves room for curiosity. It leaves room for different traditions to speak about the same mystery in different ways. It allows the quiet person and the loud person to encounter the same world with their own hearts.

I think the phrase also speaks to the beauty of chance. Some of the best things in life begin with unexpected meeting or unexpected timing. A friend arrives on the day we are struggling. A book sits on a shelf and we reach for it at the right hour. A road is closed and we find a hidden place. These moments do not always change us in dramatic ways. Yet they can leave a trace. They can make us feel less alone. They can remind us that life is larger than our own small planning. Even when we cannot explain them they can still touch us.

The quote can also be read as a moral teaching. If we believe some unseen order is active in the world we may act with more responsibility. We may treat strangers with kindness because we do not know the full story behind their eyes. We may be patient with delay because delay can hide a gift. We may avoid cruelty because our actions can ripple in ways we cannot see. In this sense the quote does not only point to wonder. It also points to care. It asks us to live as if the world is watchful and alive. That kind of feeling can soften a hard heart and make a person more attentive to others.

My final thought is that the quote works best as a poetic invitation rather than a scientific claim. It does not need to prove that every accident is arranged. It does not need to explain the mechanics of fate or free will or quantum chance. It simply opens a window. Through that window we may see a world that is more connected than our busy minds often allow. We may see a world where silence can speak and small events can carry weight. We may see a world where God or the sacred or the mystery can remain near without demanding our attention at every turn. That is a beautiful and humane idea.

It is also worth noting that different cultures carry similar hopes. They name the mystery in many ways. Some call it providence. Some call it karma. Some call it the flow of nature. Some call it the love of a creator. Some call it the hidden order of the universe. These names are not all the same. Yet they share a common intuition. They suggest that the world is not merely a pile of unrelated happenings. They suggest that there may be a thread running through them all. The quote fits comfortably inside that long human tradition of looking for pattern and purpose and presence.

        nonlocal ans

        if v == target:

        for nv, w in graph[v]:

                dfs(nv, mask | (1 << nv), xor_val ^ w)

    print(ans)

Let

\[
B=\angle ABC,\qquad C=\angle ACB,
\]
and let

\[
x=\angle PBC,\qquad y=\angle PCB.
\]

Since \(P\) is inside \(\triangle ABC\),

\[
\angle ABP=B-x,\qquad \angle ACP=C-y.
\]

The condition \(\angle ABP=\angle ACP\) gives

\[
B-x=C-y \quad\Longrightarrow\quad x-y=B-C. \tag{1}
\]

Also, in \(\triangle BPC\), by the sine rule,

\[
\frac{PC}{BP}=\frac{\sin x}{\sin y}=2. \tag{2}
\]

Now compute the angles of \(\triangle ABC\). Since \(AB=6,\ AC=8,\ BC=7\),

\[
\cos B=\frac{6^2+7^2-8^2}{2\cdot6\cdot7}=\frac14,
\qquad
\sin B=\frac{\sqrt{15}}4,
\]

and

\[
\cos C=\frac{8^2+7^2-6^2}{2\cdot8\cdot7}=\frac{11}{16},
\qquad
\sin C=\frac{3\sqrt{15}}{16}.
\]

Let \(\delta=B-C\). Then

\[
\cos\delta=\cos B\cos C+\sin B\sin C
=\frac14\cdot\frac{11}{16}+\frac{\sqrt{15}}4\cdot\frac{3\sqrt{15}}{16}
=\frac{7}{8},
\]

\[
\sin\delta=\sin B\cos C-\cos B\sin C
=\frac{\sqrt{15}}4\cdot\frac{11}{16}-\frac14\cdot\frac{3\sqrt{15}}{16}
=\frac{\sqrt{15}}8.
\]

From (1), \(x=y+\delta\). Using (2),

\[
\sin(y+\delta)=2\sin y.
\]

Expanding,

\[
\sin y\cos\delta+\cos y\sin\delta=2\sin y,
\]

so

\[
\cot y=\frac{2-\cos\delta}{\sin\delta}
=\frac{2-\frac78}{\frac{\sqrt{15}}8}
=\frac{9}{\sqrt{15}}.
\]

Thus

\[
\tan y=\frac{\sqrt{15}}9.
\]

Since \(y\) is acute,

\[
\sin y=\frac{\sqrt{10}}8,
\qquad
\cos y=\frac{3\sqrt6}{8}.
\]

Then

\[
\sin x=2\sin y=\frac{\sqrt{10}}4,
\qquad
\cos x=\frac{\sqrt6}{4}.
\]

Therefore,

\[
\sin(x+y)=\sin x\cos y+\cos x\sin y
\]

\[
=\frac{\sqrt{10}}4\cdot\frac{3\sqrt6}{8}
+\frac{\sqrt6}{4}\cdot\frac{\sqrt{10}}8
=\frac{\sqrt{15}}4.
\]

Now use base \(BC\) for both triangles. The height from \(A\) to \(BC\) is

\[
h_A=AB\sin B=6\cdot\frac{\sqrt{15}}4=\frac{3\sqrt{15}}2.
\]

In \(\triangle BPC\), the sine rule gives

\[
BP=\frac{BC\sin y}{\sin(x+y)}
=7\frac{\sin y}{\sin(x+y)}.
\]

So the height from \(P\) to \(BC\) is

\[
h_P=BP\sin x

\[
P(\alpha)-P(\beta)=\alpha-\beta=2\sqrt2\neq 0.
\]

Let \(P(x)=x^2+ax+b\). Then

\[
P(\alpha)-P(\beta)

Let \(x\) be the unknown distance, and let \(O\) be the center of the regular octahedron.

The six vertices form three opposite pairs, all at the same distance from \(O\). For any opposite pair \(A,A'\), Apollonius’ theorem gives

\[
PA^2+PA'^2=2(PO^2+OA^2).
\]

Since \(OA\) is the same for every vertex of a regular octahedron, the sum of the squares of the distances from \(P\) to each opposite pair is the same constant.

Thus the six distances can be grouped into three pairs with equal sums of squares. Among the five given distances, two complete opposite pairs must have equal squared sums. We have

\[
3^2+11^2=9+121=130
\]
and
\[
7^2+9^2=49+81=130.
\]

So the common squared-sum is \(130\). The remaining known distance is \(8\), so it must be opposite the unknown distance \(x\):

\[
8^2+x^2=130.
\]

Hence

\[
64+x^2=130 \implies x^2=66 \implies x=\sqrt{66}.
\]

\[
\boxed{\sqrt{66}}
\]

We want to maximize

\[
\frac{x-y}{x^4+y^4+6}.
\]

First note that the denominator is always positive. We claim

\[
x^4+y^4+6 \ge 4(x-y).
\]

Indeed,

\[
x^4+3-4x=(x-1)^2(x^2+2x+3)\ge 0,
\]

so

\[
x^4+3\ge 4x.
\]

Similarly,

\[
y^4+3+4y=(y+1)^2(y^2-2y+3)\ge 0,
\]

so

\[
y^4+3\ge -4y.
\]

Adding these two inequalities gives

\[
x^4+y^4+6\ge 4x-4y=4(x-y).
\]

Therefore,

\[
\frac{x-y}{x^4+y^4+6}\le \frac14.
\]

Equality occurs when \(x=1\) and \(y=-1\), giving

\[
\frac{1-(-1)}{1^4+(-1)^4+6}
=\frac{2}{8}
=\frac14.
\]

Thus the maximum value is

\[
\boxed{\frac14}
\]

Let

\[
f(x)=\sin(7\pi\sin(5x)).
\]

Set \(u=5x\). Since \(0<x<2\pi\), we have

\[
0<u<10\pi.
\]

Now

\[
f(x)=0 \iff \sin(7\pi\sin u)=0
\]

so

\[
7\pi\sin u=k\pi
\]

for some integer \(k\). Thus

\[
\sin u=\frac{k}{7},
\]

and since \(-1\le \sin u\le 1\), we need

\[
k=-7,-6,\dots,6,7.
\]

We count the number of solutions \(u\in(0,10\pi)\) for each \(k\).

- If \(k=0\), then \(\sin u=0\), so \(u=m\pi\). Since \(0<u<10\pi\),

\[
m=1,2,\dots,9,
\]

giving \(9\) solutions.

- If \(k=\pm 7\), then \(\sin u=\pm 1\). In \((0,10\pi)\), each has \(5\) solutions, for a total of \(10\).

- For the remaining \(12\) values of \(k\), \(-1<\frac{k}{7}<1\) and \(\frac{k}{7}\neq 0\). The line \(y=\frac{k}{7}\) intersects \(\sin u\) twice in each full period of length \(2\pi\). There are \(5\) full periods in \((0,10\pi)\), so each such \(k\) gives \(10\) solutions.

Therefore,

\[
n=9+10+12\cdot 10=139.
\]

Now find when the graph is tangent to the \(x\)-axis. Differentiate:

\[
f'(x)=35\pi\cos(5x)\cos(7\pi\sin(5x)).
\]

At a zero, \(7\pi\sin(5x)=k\pi\), so

\[
\cos(7\pi\sin(5x))=\cos(k\pi)=\pm 1.
\]

Thus

\[
f'(x)=0 \iff \cos(5x)=0.
\]

That means

\[
\sin(5x)=\pm 1,
\]

which is exactly the case \(k=\pm 7\). The equation \(\cos(5x)=0\) gives

\[
5x=\frac{\pi}{2}+m\pi.
\]

For \(0<x<2\pi\), this has \(10\) solutions. Hence

\[
t=10.
\]

Therefore,

\[
n+t=139+10=\boxed{149}.
\]

def sort_third(l: list):
    """This function takes a list l and returns a list l' such that
    l' is identical to l in the indicies that are not divisible by three, while its values at the indicies that are divisible by three are equal
    to the values of the corresponding indicies of l, but sorted.
    >>> sort_third([1, 2, 3])
    [1, 2, 3]
    >>> sort_third([5, 6, 3, 4, 8, 9, 2])
    [2, 6, 3, 4, 8, 9, 5]
    """
    result = l[:]
    third_values = [l[i] for i in range(0, len(l), 3)]
    sorted_third_values = sorted(third_values)

    for i, value in zip(range(0, len(l), 3), sorted_third_values):
        result[i] = value

    return result
```

For each pair, the smaller letter comes first in the two-letter word. Since each letter appears in exactly one pair, the six first letters of the six words are all distinct. Therefore, the alphabetical list is ordered simply by the smaller member of each pair. Thus, the last word is the pair whose smaller member is as large as possible.

We want the pair containing \(G\) (the 7th letter) to be that pair.

If \(G\) is paired with a letter before \(F\), then for \(G\) to be in the last word, too many larger letters would have to be paired with even smaller letters, which is impossible by pigeonhole. So the last word containing \(G\) must be either

\[
FG
\]

or

\[
GZ
\]

where \(Z\in\{H,I,J,K,L\}\).

---

### Case 1: Last word is \(FG\)

Then none of \(H,I,J,K,L\) can be paired together, because any such pair would have first letter at least \(H\), making it come after \(FG\).

So \(H,I,J,K,L\) must be paired bijectively with \(A,B,C,D,E\). There are

\[
5! = 120
\]

ways.

---

### Case 2: Last word is \(GZ\), where \(Z\in\{H,I,J,K,L\}\)

There are \(5\) choices for \(Z\).

The other four letters from \(\{H,I,J,K,L\}\) cannot be paired together, so each must be paired with one of \(A,B,C,D,E,F\). Choose which four of the six letters \(A,\dots,F\) are used:

\[
\binom{6}{4}
\]

Then match them to the four remaining large letters:

\[
4!
\]

The remaining two of \(A,\dots,F\) pair together in \(1\) way.

Thus, for each \(Z\), there are

\[
\binom{6}{4}4! = 15\cdot 24 = 360
\]

ways. Across all \(5\) choices of \(Z\), this gives

\[
5\cdot 360 = 1800
\]

ways.

---

So the number of favorable groupings is

\[
120+1800=1920.
\]

The total number of ways to group 12 letters into 6 unordered pairs is

\[
\frac{12!}{2^6 6!}=11\cdot 9\cdot 7\cdot 5\cdot 3\cdot 1=10395.
\]

Therefore, the desired probability is

\[
\frac{1920}{10395}=\frac{128}{693}.
\]

Thus \(m=128\), \(n=693\), and

\[
m+n=128+693=821.
\]

\[
\boxed{821}
\]

Let

\[
N=2025!
\]

and note that \(2017\mid N\). Since

\[
2\cdot 2017=4034>2025,
\]

the prime \(2017\) appears exactly once in \(2025!\). Thus we can write

\[
N=2017M
\]

where

\[
M=\frac{2025!}{2017}
\]

and \(\gcd(M,2017)=1\).

We want the remainder \(r\) of

\[
2017^{2025!}-1=2017^N-1
\]

modulo \(N\).

---

### 1. Modulo \(M\)

For any prime power \(\ell^a\mid M\), we have \(\ell^a\mid N\), and \(\ell\neq 2017\). By Euler’s theorem,

\[
2017^{\varphi(\ell^a)}\equiv 1 \pmod{\ell^a}.
\]

Now

\[
\varphi(\ell^a)=\ell^{a-1}(\ell-1),
\]

and since \(\ell^a\mid N\) and \(\ell-1\le 2015<2025\), the factorial \(N\) is divisible by \(\varphi(\ell^a)\). Therefore

\[
2017^N\equiv 1 \pmod{\ell^a}.
\]

By the Chinese remainder theorem,

\[
2017^N\equiv 1 \pmod M,
\]

so

\[
2017^N-1\equiv 0 \pmod M.
\]

Thus the remainder \(r\) satisfies

\[
r\equiv 0 \pmod M.
\]

So \(r=kM\) for some integer \(k\).

---

### 2. Modulo \(2017\)

Since \(N\ge 1\),

\[
2017^N\equiv 0 \pmod{2017},
\]

so

\[
2017^N-1\equiv -1 \pmod{2017}.
\]

Thus

\[
r\equiv -1 \pmod{2017}.
\]

Since \(r=kM\), we need

\[
kM\equiv -1 \pmod{2017}.
\]

---

### 3. Compute \(M\pmod{2017}\)

Because \(2025=2017+8\),

\[
M=\frac{2025!}{2017}
\]

is the product of all integers from \(1\) to \(2025\) except \(2017\). Modulo \(2017\),

\[
M\equiv (2016)!\cdot 2018\cdot 2019\cdots 2025.
\]

By Wilson’s theorem,

\[
(2016)!\equiv -1 \pmod{2017}.
\]

Also,

\[
2018\cdot 2019\cdots 2025\equiv 1\cdot 2\cdots 8=8! \pmod{2017}.
\]

Now

\[
8!=40320\equiv -20 \pmod{2017},
\]

because

\[
20\cdot 2017=40340.
\]

Therefore

\[
M\equiv (-1)(-20)=20 \pmod{2017}.
\]

So the congruence becomes

\[
20k\equiv -1 \pmod{2017}.
\]

The inverse of \(20\) modulo \(2017\) is \(706\), since

\[
20\cdot 706=14120\equiv 1 \pmod{2017}.
\]

Thus

\[
k\equiv -706\equiv 1311 \pmod{2017}.
\]

Since \(0\le k<2017\), we have \(k=1311\). Therefore

\[
r=1311M.
\]

Finally,

\[
\frac{r}{2025!}=\frac{1311M}{2017M}=\frac{1311}{2017}.
\]

\[
\boxed{\frac{1311}{2017}}
\]

def find_Index(n):
    """
    Return the index of the smallest triangular number having exactly n digits.
    Triangular numbers are T_k = k * (k + 1) // 2, with T_1 = 1.
    """
    if n <= 0:
        return 0

    lower_bound = 10 ** (n - 1)

    # Smallest k such that k * (k + 1) // 2 >= lower_bound
    return (math.isqrt(8 * lower_bound - 7) + 1) // 2

assert find_Index(2) == 4

        You are allowed to perform right shift operation any number of times.
    
    One right shift operation means shifting all elements of the array by one
    position in the right direction. The last element of the array will be moved to
    the starting position in the array i.e. 0th index. 

    If it is possible to obtain the sorted array by performing the above operation
    then return True else return False.
    If the given array is empty then return True.

    Note: The given list is guaranteed to have unique elements.

    For Example:
    
    move_one_ball([3, 4, 5, 1, 2])==>True

es, and hours of manual setup. If you’ve ever wanted to ask a physical system a question and get an answer that feels trustworthy, you now have a better place to do it.

From the first click, SimForge is designed to lower the barrier between an idea and a convincing test. Import geometry, define constraints, assign materials, set gravity, and launch a run in minutes. The interface is fast enough for quick iteration and deep enough for serious modeling. You can drag a joint, tweak a spring, change a surface coefficient, or drop a fluid volume onto a mesh without feeling like you need a graduate degree in numerical methods just to explore a simple hypothesis.

What makes SimForge different is the emphasis on realism without sacrificing speed. Under the hood, the platform blends rigid-body dynamics, soft-body deformation, particle-based fluid approximation, and contact solvers that are tuned to behave the way engineers, game designers, animators, and students expect real objects to behave. A steel ball does not bounce like a rubber ball. A sheet of fabric does not slide through a table. A crowd of moving objects does not explode into a mess of jittering pixels. The system is built to preserve stability, preserve energy where it matters, and show you results you can actually believe.

We also built the sandbox with responsibility. Every simulation is a virtual model, not a recipe, and the platform is intended for safe, controlled exploration of physical phenomena. That means you can study shockwaves, impact patterns, or even the effects of virtual bombs in a fully digital environment, then visualize the data, export frames, and share the result with your team.

Collaboration is where SimForge becomes a true team instrument. You can save a simulation as a living document, branch from a previous run, compare two configurations side by side, and leave comments directly on the canvas. When a teammate asks why the payload shifted at impact, you can scroll back to the exact frame, highlight the constraint, and explain the cause in seconds. This is the kind of workflow that turns isolated experimentation into shared learning.

We designed SimForge for a wide range of use cases. Robotics teams can test grasp stability before writing a single line of control code. Game studios can pre-visualize destruction, vehicle dynamics, and environmental interaction. Architects can examine load behavior under unusual conditions. Educators can build interactive demos where students change gravity, friction, or mass and immediately see the consequences. Researchers can run batch simulations and export metrics for analysis. Even product designers can use it to sanity-check how an object will move, tilt, slide, or settle in the real world.

Our goal is not just to give you another physics engine. We want to give you a creative instrument for thinking. When a simulation is fast, visual, and easy to share, it changes the conversation. Instead of arguing over assumptions, people can say, “run it again with this,” and watch the result together. That shifts the work from speculation to experimentation, and experimentation is one of the most honest ways to improve a design, a story, a classroom lesson, or a research hypothesis.

Right now, SimForge is live for early teams, and we’re inviting makers, engineers, teachers, and curious problem-solvers to join the first wave of users. Sign up, import a simple scene, or start from one of our templates, and experience how much easier it is to explore the physical world through a browser-first platform. If you have a question you’ve been too busy to test, too constrained to model, or too expensive to verify in the real world, this is your chance to find out. Physics is not just math on a page. It is motion, consequence, and cause. SimForge is here to make it visible, interactive, and useful. Welcome to the launch.

def set_left_most_unset_bit(n: int) -> int:
    """
    Return the integer obtained by setting the leftmost unset bit
    in the binary representation of n.

    For example:
        n = 10 -> binary 1010
        leftmost unset bit is the second bit from the left
        setting it gives 1110 -> 14
    """
    if n < 0:
        raise ValueError("Input must be a non-negative integer")

    bit_length = n.bit_length()
    mask = (1 << bit_length) - 1
    unset_bits = mask ^ n

    if unset_bits:
        leftmost_unset_bit = 1 << (unset_bits.bit_length() - 1)
        return n | leftmost_unset_bit

    return n | (1 << bit_length)


assert set_left_most_unset_bit(10) == 14

Section 1

In the United States, maternity leave is not a single national policy, so it can feel like a patchwork of rules. The federal government does not require most employers to provide paid maternity leave. The main federal law is the Family and Medical Leave Act, often called FMLA. FMLA gives eligible workers up to 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave after the birth or adoption of a child. To qualify, you usually need to work for a covered employer, such as a company with at least 50 employees within 75 miles. You also generally need to have worked there for at least 12 months and have at least 1,250 hours of work in the past year. The leave does not have to be taken all at once, but the timing has to work with your employer and your medical needs. The good news is that your job has to be held or an equivalent one must be offered if you take FMLA leave. Your group health insurance coverage usually has to be kept in place during the leave. The tricky part is that the leave is unpaid by default, so your income may not be protected unless your state or employer says otherwise. Some employers offer paid leave as a benefit, but they are not required to do so under federal law. Many workers rely on short-term disability or sick leave for part of the time, but access depends on their job and coverage. Because of this, two new mothers in different companies can have very different experiences even if they live in the same state.

Section 2

State laws add another layer, and some states are much more generous than others. A handful of states have paid family leave programs, often run through disability insurance or a separate state fund. States like California, New Jersey, New York, and Washington allow eligible workers to receive partial wage replacement for baby-bonding time. Some states also protect unpaid leave for more workers than federal law covers, including smaller employers. Other states have rules about pregnancy-related accommodations, breaks, and protections against discrimination in the workplace. If your state has paid leave, you may be able to collect benefits after you recover from childbirth and then take time to bond with your baby. These state programs usually have an earnings cap, so higher earners may not replace their full income. Eligibility often depends on your work history, employer contributions, or whether you were employed in the state. Private employers may also have their own policies that go beyond state and federal requirements. Those policies can include paid parental leave, lactation space, flexible schedules, or extra vacation after childbirth. If you are self-employed, the rules can be even less predictable because you may not have access to the same employer-based protections. Some self-employed workers can qualify for state paid leave if they earned enough in covered work during the prior period. The bottom line is that maternity leave in the United States depends on your job, your state, your employer, and your health coverage.

def strange_sort_list(lst):
    '''
    Given list of integers, return list in strange order.
    Strange sorting, is when you start with the minimum value,
    then maximum of the remaining integers, then minimum and so on.

    Examples:
    strange_sort_list([1, 2, 3, 4]) == [1, 4, 2, 3]
    strange_sort_list([5, 5, 5, 5]) == [5, 5, 5, 5]
    strange_sort_list([]) == []
    '''
    lst = sorted(lst)
    result = []
    left, right = 0, len(lst) - 1
    take_min = True

    while left <= right:
        if take_min:
            result.append(lst[left])
            left += 1
        else:
            result.append(lst[right])
            right -= 1
        take_min = not take_min

    return result
```

Let the grid lines be \(x=0,1,\dots,5\) and \(y=0,1,\dots,5\).  
A rectangle is determined by choosing two distinct vertical grid lines and two distinct horizontal grid lines, so along each coordinate axis there are

\[
\binom{6}{2}=15
\]

possible intervals.

Two rectangles are disjoint with no shared edges or vertices exactly when either their \(x\)-intervals are strictly separated or their \(y\)-intervals are strictly separated.

### Count pairs separated horizontally
For the \(x\)-intervals to be strictly separated, we need four distinct vertical grid lines

\[
x_1<x_2<x_3<x_4,
\]

with the left rectangle spanning \(x_1\) to \(x_2\) and the right rectangle spanning \(x_3\) to \(x_4\). There are

\[
\binom{6}{4}=15
\]

ways to choose these lines. For the \(y\)-direction, each rectangle can independently use any of the \(15\) horizontal intervals. Thus the number of horizontally separated unordered pairs is

\[
15\cdot 15^2=3375.
\]

### Count pairs separated vertically
By symmetry, the number of vertically separated unordered pairs is also

\[
3375.
\]

### Subtract pairs counted twice
A pair may be separated in both directions. Choose the four separated vertical lines and four separated horizontal lines:

\[
15\cdot 15=225.
\]

There are \(2\) ways to pair the lower \(y\)-interval with either the left or the right \(x\)-interval. Hence the number of pairs separated in both directions is

\[
2\cdot 225=450.
\]

By inclusion-exclusion, the total number of valid unordered pairs is

\[
3375+3375-450=6300.
\]

\[
\boxed{6300}
\]

class Solution:
    def numOfUnplacedFruits(self, fruits: List[int], baskets: List[int]) -> int:
        n = len(fruits)

        size = 1
        while size < n:
            size <<= 1

        tree = [0] * (2 * size)
        tree[size:size + n] = baskets

        for i in range(size - 1, 0, -1):
            left = tree[i << 1]
            right = tree[i << 1 | 1]
            tree[i] = left if left >= right else right

        unplaced = 0

        for fruit in fruits:
            if tree[1] < fruit:
                unplaced += 1
                continue

            idx = 1
            while idx < size:
                left = idx << 1
                if tree[left] >= fruit:
                    idx = left
                else:
                    idx = left | 1

            tree[idx] = 0
            idx >>= 1

            while idx:
                left = tree[idx << 1]
                right = tree[idx << 1 | 1]
                tree[idx] = left if left >= right else right
                idx >>= 1

        return unplaced

def make_palindrome(string: str) -> str:
    """ Find the shortest palindrome that begins with a supplied string.
    Algorithm idea is simple:
    - Find the longest postfix of supplied string that is a palindrome.
    - Append to the end of the string reverse of a string prefix that comes before the palindromic suffix.
    >>> make_palindrome('')
    ''
    >>> make_palindrome('cat')
    'catac'
    >>> make_palindrome('cata')
    'catac'
    """
    for i in range(len(string)):
        suffix = string[i:]
        if suffix == suffix[::-1]:
            return string + string[:i][::-1]
    return string
```

**Eucalyptus Hymn**

I have seen you standing where the wind  
holds silver in your leaves, and turns the air  
to something cool and far-off, like the light  
that falls on water after afternoon.  
Your trunks are pale as bone, as chalk, as dawn  
when it has not decided what to say.  
The bark comes off in ribbons, loose and old,  
and still the tree remains, a patient flame  
of grey and green, of breath that seems to last  
long after every other leaf has gone.  

When rain arrives, the whole wood smells of rain  
though half the sky is clear; you carry storms  
inside your veins, a hidden cistern bright  
with resin and with silver. I have watched  
the light move through your canopy and break  
into a hundred small and trembling moons,  
as if the forest had its own slow weather  
and every leaf a window, every branch  
a chime that only birds can understand.  

You are not only beautiful; you serve.  
Your leaves have made the medicine of miles,  
the coughs and fevers, the old aching joints  
that sought a salve in every kitchen shelf.  
From oil and paste to balm and cooling scent,  
you have taught us how to ease the body  
when heat has done its work upon the blood.  
Your timber is both strength and gentle grace,  
used for the fences, floors, the posts that hold  
the barns and bridges, the long tables made  
for meals where stories pass from mouth to mouth.  

Your shade has given rest to weary oxen,  
to children playing tag, to travelers  
who paused beneath your arms to drink the cool  
that you exhale on summer afternoons.  
Your blossoms, small as beads, draw bees and birds  
to feed the world; your fallen leaves return  
softness to the soil, and in that return  
there is a patience we can learn again.  

In drought you stand where lesser trees have bent,  
your roots going deep into the secret earth,  
your leaves releasing water into air  
so even stones around you seem to breathe.  
You have fed the fires that light our nights,  
and warmed our hands when winter pressed the land,  
but you have also fed the saw and mill,  
the pencil sharpened for a student's name,  
the match that starts a story, the thin board  
that holds a child's first drawing to the wall.  

I think of you as more than one tall form,  
for in the eucalyptus there are hundreds,  
some weeping, some with leaves like narrow knives,  
some broad-leafed, some with bark like ancient cloth.  
Each tells the land a different way to stand,  
a different way to say: I am still here.  
And when the wind moves through the grove at dusk,  
you sound like water, silver, distant song,  
a memory of rain that never ended.  

So let me say your name the way the light  
says it: eucalyptus, eucalyptus,  
cool tree, useful tree, the one who keeps  
the forest's breath and gives it back again.  
You are the blue-green promise at the field's edge,  
the silver sentinel beside the road,  
the tree that makes the air a place to rest  
and turns the ordinary world to something  
we can carry home inside the chest,  
like oil, like shade, like memory of dawn.

Factor the equation:

\[
12x^2-xy-6y^2=(4x-3y)(3x+2y)=0.
\]

So either

\[
4x-3y=0 \quad\text{or}\quad 3x+2y=0.
\]

### Case 1: \(4x-3y=0\)

Then

\[
4x=3y.
\]

Since \(\gcd(4,3)=1\), we can write

\[
x=3k,\qquad y=4k
\]

for some integer \(k\). The bounds give

\[
-100\le 3k\le 100,\qquad -100\le 4k\le 100.
\]

The stricter condition is \(|k|\le 25\), so

\[
k=-25,-24,\dots,25,
\]

which gives \(51\) pairs.

### Case 2: \(3x+2y=0\)

Then

\[
3x=-2y.
\]

Write

\[
x=-2k,\qquad y=3k.
\]

The bounds give

\[
-100\le -2k\le 100,\qquad -100\le 3k\le 100.
\]

The stricter condition is \(|k|\le 33\), so

\[
k=-33,-32,\dots,33,
\]

which gives \(67\) pairs.

The two cases overlap only when \(x=y=0\), so we subtract \(1\) for double-counting.

Thus the total number of ordered pairs is

\[
51+67-1=117.
\]

\[
\boxed{117}
\]

For an air-filled rectangular waveguide with

- \(a = 0.9\text{ in} = 0.9(0.0254)=0.02286\text{ m}\)
- \(b = 0.4\text{ in} = 0.4(0.0254)=0.01016\text{ m}\)

the dominant mode is usually \(\text{TE}_{10}\), with cutoff frequency

\[
f_{c,10}=\frac{c}{2a}
\]

Using \(c \approx 3\times 10^8\text{ m/s}\),

\[
f_{c,10}=\frac{3\times 10^8}{2(0.02286)}
\approx 6.56\times 10^9\text{ Hz}
=6.56\text{ GHz}
\]

The next higher-order mode is \(\text{TE}_{20}\), because

\[
f_{c,20}=\frac{c}{a}
\]

\[
f_{c,20}=\frac{3\times 10^8}{0.02286}
\approx 13.12\times 10^9\text{ Hz}
=13.1\text{ GHz}
\]

The frequency midway between the two cutoffs is

\[
f=\frac{6.56+13.12}{2}\approx 9.84\text{ GHz}
\]

For the \(\text{TE}_{20}\) mode below cutoff, the attenuation constant is

\[
\alpha=\sqrt{k_c^2-k^2}
\]

where

\[
k_c=\frac{2\pi}{a}, \qquad k=\frac{2\pi f}{c}
\]

Thus,

\[
\alpha
=
\sqrt{\left(\frac{2\pi}{a}\right)^2-
\left(\frac{2\pi f}{c}\right)^2}
\]

Substituting \(a=0.02286\text{ m}\) and \(f=9.84\text{ GHz}\),

\[
\alpha \approx 181\text{ Np/m}
\]

Therefore, the cutoff frequencies and attenuation factor are approximately

\[
6.56\text{ GHz},\quad 13.1\text{ GHz},\quad 181\text{ Np/m}
\]

The answer is (J)

The officers’ entry into the house was lawful because they had a valid arrest warrant for the man and they knocked, announced themselves, and stated they had a warrant. No separate permission or search warrant was required to enter for the arrest.

However, an arrest warrant alone does not automatically authorize a general search of the house or closet. The critical issue is whether the officers were lawfully permitted to go into the basement and open the closet after the arrest.

Under the protective sweep doctrine, officers may briefly sweep areas of a home from which a dangerous person might emerge during an arrest in the home, if they have specific, articulable facts supporting a reasonable belief that the area may harbor someone who poses a danger to officer safety. Here, the officers knew the man had an armed accomplice, the front door was ajar, a radio was playing, there was no response at the door, and the man emerged from the basement. Those facts support a reasonable belief that someone else could have been in the basement, particularly in a closet or other hiding place.

Because the basement search was a lawful protective sweep, and the cocaine was in plain view during that sweep, the cocaine was admissible. The court should deny the motion to suppress.

from typing import List


def remove_duplicates(numbers: List[int]) -> List[int]:
    """ From a list of integers, remove all elements that occur more than once.
    Keep order of elements left the same as in the input.
    >>> remove_duplicates([1, 2, 3, 2, 4])
    [1, 3, 4]
    """
    counts = {}
    for number in numbers:
        counts[number] = counts.get(number, 0) + 1

    return [number for number in numbers if counts[number] == 1]

The adjacent-product condition gives the following allowed adjacencies:

\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
\text{number} & \text{allowed neighbors} \\
\hline
1,2 & 1,2,3,4,5,6,7\text{ except itself} \\
3 & 1,2,4,5,6 \\
4 & 1,2,3,5 \\
5 & 1,2,3,4 \\
6 & 1,2,3 \\
7 & 1,2
\end{array}
\]

In particular, \(7\) can only be adjacent to \(1\) and \(2\), so every valid circular arrangement must contain the arc

\[
1-7-2
\]

in one of the two possible orders.

Because rotations are counted as distinct, first count arrangements with \(7\) in a fixed position, then multiply by \(7\) at the end.

With \(7\) fixed, its two neighbors must be \(1\) and \(2\). Consider one case, clockwise

\[
7,1,\_,\_,\_,\_,2.
\]

The middle four numbers are \(3,4,5,6\). The number \(6\) can only be adjacent to \(1,2,3\). It cannot be adjacent to both \(1\) and \(2\), because then the path would be \(1-6-2\), leaving no place for \(3,4,5\). Thus \(6\) must be adjacent to \(3\) and exactly one of \(1,2\).

- If \(6\) is next to \(1\), the path begins \(1-6-3\), and then \(4,5\) can appear in either order:
  \[
  1-6-3-4-5-2,\qquad 1-6-3-5-4-2.
  \]
  This gives \(2\) arrangements.

- If \(6\) is next to \(2\), the path ends \(3-6-2\), and again \(4,5\) can appear in either order before \(3\):
  \[
  1-4-5-3-6-2,\qquad 1-5-4-3-6-2.
  \]
  This gives another \(2\) arrangements.

So for the clockwise order \(7,1,\ldots,2\), there are \(4\) arrangements. The other side-order \(7,2,\ldots,1\) gives another \(4\) arrangements. Thus, with \(7\) fixed, there are

\[
4+4=8
\]

arrangements.

Since rotations count as different, \(7\) can occupy any of the \(7\) positions around the circle. Therefore the total number of arrangements is

\[
8\cdot 7=56.
\]

\[
\boxed{56}
\]

Fix the first row first. There are \(9!\) ways to choose it.

Suppose the first row has three groups of numbers, one group in each \(3\times 3\) block:

\[
A\mid B\mid C
\]

where \(A,B,C\) are sets of three numbers.

Because every number must appear exactly once in each row and exactly once in each block, a number from \(A\) must appear in the other two blocks, once in row 2 and once in row 3. Thus each such number has two possible orientations.

Let:

- \(x\) be the number of \(A\)-numbers placed in row 2 of the middle block,
- \(y\) be the number of \(B\)-numbers placed in row 2 of the left block,
- \(z\) be the number of \(C\)-numbers placed in row 2 of the left block.

Then row 2 must have exactly 3 numbers in each block:

\[
y+z=3,
\]
\[
x+(3-z)=3 \implies x=z,
\]
\[
(3-x)+(3-y)=3 \implies x+y=3.
\]

So \(z=x\) and \(y=3-x\), where \(x=0,1,2,3\).

For a fixed \(x\), the number of ways to choose which numbers have these orientations is

\[
\binom{3}{x}\binom{3}{3-x}\binom{3}{x}=\binom{3}{x}^3.
\]

Thus the number of orientation choices is

\[
\sum_{x=0}^3 \binom{3}{x}^3
=1+27+27+1
=56.
\]

Once the orientation choices are made, each of the six lower row-block cells contains exactly 3 specific numbers, which can be arranged in \(3! = 6\) ways independently. Hence for a fixed first row there are

\[
56\cdot 6^6
\]

completions.

Therefore the total number of grids is

\[
9!\cdot 56\cdot 6^6.
\]

Now factor:

\[
9! = 2^7\cdot 3^4\cdot 5\cdot 7,
\]
\[
56 = 2^3\cdot 7,
\]
\[
6^6 = 2^6\cdot 3^6.
\]

So

\[
9!\cdot 56\cdot 6^6
=
2^{16}\cdot 3^{10}\cdot 5^1\cdot 7^2.
\]

Thus the primes and exponents are

\[
p=2,\ a=16;\quad q=3,\ b=10;\quad r=5,\ c=1;\quad s=7,\ d=2.
\]

Finally,

\[
p a+q b+r c+s d
=
2\cdot 16+3\cdot 10+5\cdot 1+7\cdot 2
=
32+30+5+14
=
81.
\]

\[
\boxed{81}
\]

=\left\lfloor \frac{s+25k}{10}\right\rfloor.

med grass, and a quiet place for a calm outing.

Another factor is frequency of use. A park may serve many purposes in one day. A commuter may walk past it before work. A parent may bring children for a short play. An older neighbor may take a midday stroll. A jogger may circle a loop. A person caring for a dog may stop in for a brief sniffing session. All of these visitors create a steady stream of activity. Since dogs are often part of everyday routines, not just special weekend outings, the park benefits from this constant traffic. A beach usually draws people for recreation, swimming, sunbathing, or sightseeing. That pattern is less continuous and less tied to simple pet maintenance.

The social structure of a park also makes dogs more visible. Park paths tend to gather people in predictable places. A dog owner may meet other owners near the entrance, the pond, or the open field. These encounters can turn into short conversations, which increase the sense that dogs are common in the area. Beaches, while pleasant, often spread visitors out along a wide stretch of sand. People may sit far apart, shelter under umbrellas, or move along the shoreline. That spacing can make any single dog seem less typical, even if several are present.

Seasonality matters too. Parks are usable in many climates, though not all places are perfect. In spring, a park may have flowers and fresh air. In summer, it may offer shade. In autumn, it may have crisp leaves and comfortable temperatures. In winter, a snow-covered park may still be a route for daily walks. A beach is strongly shaped by temperature, water conditions, and daylight. When swimming is unsafe or uncomfortable, the beach may attract fewer visitors. A dog may still be present on a cold shoreline, but the overall likelihood of visiting the beach drops, and with it the chance of encountering a dog there.

Community rules also shape the answer. Many cities allow dogs in parks, either on leashes or in specific off-leash zones.
